original_text: Reproductive Strategies A flower produces two types of spores Microspore-Male gametophyte Undergoes mitosis Becomes pollen grain Megaspore-Female gametophyte Undergoes mitosis Becomes the female gametophyte, an embryo sac within an ovulewithin an ovary Ovule becomes a seed Ovary becomes a fruit
explanation: Flowering plants are heterosporous, producing two distinct types of spores: 1) Microspores: male spores that develop in the anther. A microspore undergoes mitosis to become a pollen grain, which is the male gametophyte. 2) Megaspores: female spores that develop in the ovary. A megaspore undergoes mitosis to become the female gametophyte (embryo sac), which is housed inside an ovule within the ovary. After fertilization, the ovule matures into a seed, and the ovary develops into a fruit.

questions.q: What structure is formed when a microspore undergoes mitosis?
questions.exp: The microspore undergoes mitosis to become a pollen grain, which represents the male gametophyte.

questions.q: Following fertilization, what do the ovule and the ovary become, respectively?
opts: The seed coat and the embryo
The pollen grain and the embryo sac
questions.exp: The ovule matures to become the seed, and the ovary matures to become the fruit.
